title: Online partnering and family related outcomes in Germany
authors: Mirkka Danielsbacka; Antti O. Tanskanen; Francesco C. Billari
exposure_measure: Met current partner ONLINE vs OFFLINE (venue of meeting; internet in general, not only dating sites)
outcome_measure: relationship satisfaction; intention to separate; separation; moving in together; intention to have a first/another child; entry into parenthood
design: between-person regressions with forward-lagged dependent variables; 4 nested models adding covariates incl. Big Five
identification_source: none — no exogenous variation; meeting venue is chosen
fulltext_reason: THE ONLY study in the frame estimating an online-meeting exposure against a realized fertility outcome. It is observational and the authors say so.
notes: THE CHAPTER TURNS ON THIS PAPER. (1) Actual first birth: NULL in the youngest cohort in every model; POSITIVE in the OLDEST cohort (interaction +0.11, p=0.006, fully adjusted). (2) Intention to have a first child: POSITIVE and robust (+0.07, p=0.017 fully adjusted). (3) Separation: HIGHER for online-met in the youngest cohort in models 1 and 4 but not model 2. (4) Satisfaction, intention to separate, moving in together: all null after full adjustment. SO THE ONE STUDY IN THE DEFINING CELL POINTS THE OPPOSITE WAY TO v5 ON BIRTHS AND INTENTIONS, AND v5's WAY ONLY ON SEPARATION. (5) THE AUTHORS RUN THE REVERSE TEST THEMSELVES: higher fertility intentions at baseline predict meeting a new partner online in the next wave, beta=0.22, p=0.001, CI 0.092-0.343 — ROUGHLY THREE TIMES the forward coefficient of 0.07 from the same data. This is the version-of-record caveat too: this is the working paper; the Journal of Family Studies version is P0 and unread.

title: A Spatial Analysis of Factors Affecting Total Fertility Rates in OECD Countries: The Role of Digitalization
exposure_measure: Fixed broadband subscriptions per 100 people; mobile broadband penetration and ICT goods exports as robustness
design: spatial panel econometrics (spatial error model) vs non-spatial fixed effects
identification_source: none — macro association with spatial dependence modelled
fulltext_reason: Macro association, no identification, and the ecological inference problem is severe at country-year level.
notes: ROBUST POSITIVE association between digitalization and REALIZED fertility at the macro level, against v5. Also finds an inverted-U in income per capita. Treat as a bound on the sign of the aggregate correlation, not as an effect estimate — country-year broadband against country-year TFR cannot separate the technology from everything else that trends with it.

title: Internet and Partnership Formation in the United States
authors: Martin Kolk; Francesco C. Billari (DisCont project)
population: US young adults, heterosexual and homosexual
fulltext_reason: Nationally representative, two data sources, and the outcome is union formation itself.
notes: AGE-DEPENDENT AND THAT IS THE FINDING: the association is NEGATIVE at younger ages (delayed partnership formation) and turns POSITIVE from the mid-to-late 20s, for both heterosexual and homosexual partnerships. Authors read it as the Internet FACILITATING union formation once people feel ready to commit. So it supports v5 at young ages and contradicts it at older ones, which is a shape no single sign can summarise. Duplicate pair: W3096306306 is the version of record and W3215766353 its preprint — DO NOT POOL.

title: Online Distance Education and Transition to Parenthood Among Female University Students in Sweden
exposure_measure: ONLINE DISTANCE education enrolment vs CAMPUS enrolment vs non-enrolment
fulltext_reason: Large register study with a clean fertility outcome, but the technology here is educational delivery, not partner search. Shared with C.3.b as well as C.2.h.
notes: Hazard of first-parity conception is 70% LOWER during campus enrolment but only 43% lower during DISTANCE enrolment, both against non-enrolment. So the online mode ATTENUATES the postponement effect of being a student — technology raising fertility relative to its offline counterpart. Directionally against v5, but the mechanism is enrolment flexibility rather than partner search, and PI Call 2 may put it wholly in C.3.b.

title: The Impact of Fertility Information Browsing on College Students’ Fertility Intentions—The Mediating Role of Parenting Sense of Competence
exposure_measure: Browsing positive vs negative fertility information online
fulltext_reason: Cross-sectional, small, single-institution, self-reported exposure and outcome.
notes: Positive fertility information beta=+0.058 (p<0.001), NEGATIVE fertility information beta=-0.749 (p<0.001) on fertility intentions. The asymmetry is the interesting part — negative online content is an order of magnitude more predictive than positive — but the design cannot separate content exposure from prior disposition.

title: Offline social capital, online social capital, and fertility intentions: evidence from China
authors: Jing Zhao; Zhijie Zou; Jianfei Chen; Yujia Chen; Wanfa Lin; Xianbo Pei; Enjing Li; Yajing Dong; Xiaoli Chen

title: Nonparametric estimation of matching efficiency and elasticity in a marriage agency platform: 2014–2025
data_source: IBJ, Japan's largest structured matching platform (search, dating and matching logs)
population: Platform users selected into serious marriage search; covers 3.3% of national marriages annually
exposure_measure: Digital intermediation of marriage search on a structured platform
outcome_measure: monthly matching efficiency and matching elasticities
identification_source: none — descriptive of the matching function over time
fulltext_reason: Direct measurement of the CONVERSION quantity v5 claims falls, on a platform covering 3.3% of Japanese marriages.
notes: MATCHING EFFICIENCY TRIPLES BETWEEN 2014 AND 2025, with diverging elasticities indicating increasingly asymmetric responsiveness. This is the single most direct measurement of v5's claimed quantity anywhere in the readable set — conversion of search into confirmed engagements — and it moves the OPPOSITE way, in the lowest-fertility rich country in the sample. Caveat that decides its weight: users are HIGHLY SELECTED into serious marriage search by costly screening, so it measures the efficiency of an intermediary chosen by people who have already decided to marry, not the conversion rate of casual app use.
